Re: ​
Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Patient Protection and Affordable Care 
Act; Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs for Medicare 
Advantage Organizations, Medicaid Managed Care Plans, State Medicaid Agencies, 
Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) Agencies and CHIP Managed Care 
Entities and Issuers of Qualified Health Plans on the Federally-Facilitated 
Exchanges (RIN 0938-AV44)  
 
Dear Administrator Oz:  
Genentech appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Medicare and Medicaid Programs; 
Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act; Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization 
for Drugs for Medicare Advantage Organizations, Medicaid Managed Care Plans, State 
Medicaid Agencies, Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) Agencies and CHIP Managed 
Care Entities, and Issuers of Qualified Health Plans on the Federally-Facilitated Exchanges 
Proposed Rule.1  
For five decades, Genentech has been fueled by a passion for science, driving us to explore 
uncharted territory and deliver groundbreaking discoveries that have fundamentally changed 
patients’ lives and reduced the burden of complex health challenges on society. As the original 
biotech company, we honor our 50-year legacy by applying the same innovative spirit—the one 
that creates life-changing therapies— to improve healthcare access and outcomes, ensuring our 
scientific breakthroughs have a real and positive impact on people’s lives. Over the past 16 years, 
we have launched 27 new medicines for patients battling devastating diseases, including cancer, 
1 91 Fed. Reg. 19890 (April 14, 2026). 
1 
 
multiple sclerosis, and hemophilia. Today, we have more than 40 approved medicines on the U.S. 
market and an additional 66 new molecules in clinical development. Furthermore, we have been 
granted 43 FDA Breakthrough Therapy Designations, reflecting our ongoing commitment to 
developing treatments with the potential to provide substantial improvements over current 
standards of care. 
Genentech supports and incorporates by reference herein the policy and other arguments detailed 
in the comments on this proposed rule filed by the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers 
of America (“PhRMA”). For this response letter, we will focus our comments on the issues and 
questions raised by the step therapy RFI. Specifically, we recommend that CMS: 
●​ Require public reporting of step therapy metrics and categorically prohibit the embedding 
of step therapy protocols within standard prior authorization criteria; 
●​ Require plans to disaggregate utilization management data by specific therapeutic areas 
to ensure accountability across patient populations; 
●​ Ensure payers across public and commercial markets actively ingest and apply 
Payer-to-Payer API-transmitted data to programmatically identify therapies a patient has 
already tried and failed; 
●​ Honor historical step therapy determinations completed under a preceding health plan; 
●​ Grant a step therapy exception when the patient has already tried and failed the required 
protocol or it is contraindicated, when the protocol is expected to be ineffective and 
delaying effective treatment would lead to severe or irreversible health consequences, 
when the protocol prevents the patient from fulfilling daily or occupational duties, or 
when the patient is currently stable on their medication; 
●​ Extend the regulatory "look-back" period used in Part D to define a "new start" patient 
from 108 days to 365 days and apply this requirement to all segments, including 
commercial plans; 
●​ Prohibit the implementation of off-label step therapy; 
●​ Anchor coverage criteria in consensus-based, peer-reviewed clinical guidelines rather 
than internal pharmacy committee directives; and,  
●​ Assert regulatory scrutiny over AI-driven claims management to ensure that AI and 
algorithms are only utilized to approve care or predict clinical pathways, and that any 
denial of coverage involves a meaningful, documented human clinical review by a peer 
specialist. 
Utilization Management Can Help Ensure Responsible Healthcare Spending, but Often 
Serves as a Barrier to Timely and Appropriate Care 
While utilization management (UM) techniques are intended to facilitate cost-effective care, the 
increasing use of opaque, inflexible, and administratively burdensome UM practices—most 
notably prior authorization and step therapy—has increasingly functioned as a systemic barrier to 
2 
 
timely patient access across both public and private insurance markets. Over the past decade and 
a half, the pervasiveness of these restrictive practices has scaled dramatically; the proportion of 
covered medicines subject to such utilization controls in Medicare Part D has effectively 
doubled, currently encompassing up to 56 percent of brand drugs.2 Compounding this expansion 
is the growing deployment of "embedded" step therapy, wherein payers obscure rigid 
treatment-sequence protocols beneath the facade of standard prior authorization criteria.3 By 
masking these automatic coverage denials and forcing patients to try and fail alternative 
regimens before gaining access to prescribed therapies, these practices fundamentally undermine 
clinical decision-making and leave providers navigating a highly unpredictable, non-transparent 
coverage landscape. 
The operational deployment of these tactics can compromise patient care by delaying access to 
clinically appropriate regimens, frequently via criteria that arbitrarily extend beyond 
FDA-approved labeling.4 Across both the commercial and Part D segments, initial coverage 
denials have become a systemic default; empirical data indicates that commercial insurers deny 
initial coverage for three out of four patients prescribed essential medications across key chronic 
disease states, triggering prolonged treatment gaps averaging three to five weeks.5 In egregious 
cases, patients are forced to cycle through as many as ten alternative therapies before receiving 
their intended treatment.6 This clinical disruption is equally pronounced within the Medicare 
Advantage (MA) sector, where 94 percent of providers report that step therapy directly restricts 
access to preferred, physician-administered Part B treatments.7  
The system-wide ramifications of unchecked utilization management are profound, degrading 
clinical outcomes, worsening health disparities, and imposing severe administrative friction 
across the care continuum. Both CMS itself and leading clinical organizations recognize that 
artificial delays in treatment can catalyze rapid disease progression, a risk that carries

ge

Available at:

ly-insured-patients-in-five-chronic-therapeutic-areas

Criteria with Clinical Treatment Guidelines. Available at: 
https://www.healthaffairs.org/doi/10.1377/hlthaff.2024.01484 
3 Blasch K.S. et al. (March 2025). Part D Prior Authorization Policies May Include Step Therapy. Avalere Health 
Advisory. Available at: 
https://advisory.avalerehealth.com/insights/part-d-prior-authorization-policies-may-include-step-therapy 
2 Avalere Health Advisory. (November 2025). Part D Formulary Management Tightens in 2026. Available at: 
https://advisory.avalerehealth.com/insights/part-d-formulary-management-tightens-in-2026 
3 
 
catastrophic implications for individuals managing severe, progressive, or autoimmune 
conditions. Furthermore, these barriers exacerbate existing health inequities, falling 
disproportionately on marginalized groups; data reveals that 56 percent of Black Americans and 
60 percent of Hispanic Americans experience utilization management restrictions, compared to 
36 percent of white Americans.8 In addition to patient impacts, inappropriate UM impacts the 
healthcare workforce, with 93 percent of physicians reporting associated care delays and 89 
percent reporting heightened professional burnout, while the broader healthcare ecosystem 
expends an estimated $93 billion annually merely to navigate and contest these administrative 
hurdles.9,10 
Ultimately, the compounding reliance on aggressive utilization management mechanisms can 
worsen the broader crisis surrounding healthcare affordability and patient access. When arbitrary 
insurance barriers intercept care, patients are frequently forced to abandon their benefits entirely 
and pay completely out-of-pocket, exposing them to significant financial vulnerability.11 While 
certain commercial payers have publicly pledged to reform prior authorization frameworks, these 
voluntary commitments conspicuously exclude prescription medications, leaving a critical 
regulatory gap across commercial, Medicare, and Medicaid formularies. To mitigate the 
escalating risk of adverse clinical outcomes and compromised medication adherence, it is 
imperative that CMS enact robust, enforceable policies centered on transparency and 
accountability, ensuring all step therapy protocols are strictly evidence-based, clinically flexible, 
and aligned with patient-centered care. 
CMS Should Require Public Reporting of Step Therapy Protocols and Eliminate "Embedded" 
Restrictions Disguised as Prior Authorization 
For utilization management frameworks to function efficiently and equitably, criteria must be 
wholly transparent and unambiguously communicated to both beneficiaries and prescribers. At 
present, both public and commercial health plans routinely obfuscate their coverage restrictions 
by concealing rigid treatment-sequence mandates within broader prior authorization 
requirements. A recent analysis of patient access to certain breast cancer treatments revealed that 
Part D sponsors required prior authorization for these therapies 97 percent of the time. However, 
up to 88 percent of these cases effectively deployed "embedded" step therapy without ever 
disclosing the existence of step therapy in their formularies.12 Such hidden administrative

https://www.fightcancer.org/sites/default/files/acs_can_part_d_formulary_analysis_final.pdf. 
 
11 IQVIA. (April 2026). U.S. Medicine Use Trends 2026. Available here 
10 Howell S., Yin P.T., Robinson J.C. (August 2021). Quantifying the Economic Burden of Drug Utilization 
Management on Payers, Manufacturers, Physicians, and Patients. Health Affairs. Available at: 
https://www.healthaffairs.org/doi/10.1377/hlthaff.2021.00036 
9 American Medical Association. (2024). 2024 Prior Authorization Physician Survey. Available at: 
https://www.ama-assn.org/system/files/prior-authorization-survey.pdf 
8 PhRMA. (October 2021). Barriers to Health Care Access in the Patient Experience. Available at: 
https://cdn.aglty.io/phrma/policy-issues/health-insurance/PES%20Report_100621_Final.pdf 
4 
 
barriers obstruct access to medically necessary oncology treatments, exposing patients to 
unanticipated treatment delays and the potential for clinical deterioration. To rectify this systemic 
opacity, CMS should require plans to publicly report step therapy metrics with the same rigor 
proposed for prior authorization, and categorically prohibit the embedding of step therapy 
protocols within otherwise typical prior authorization criteria. Finally, to prevent localized health 
inequities from being obscured by aggregated reporting, CMS must require plans to disaggregate 
their utilization management data by specific therapeutic areas, ensuring accountability across all 
patient populations. 
Use of the Payer-to-Payer APIs Can Promote Continuity of Care Across Payers 
The payer practice of ignoring a beneficiary's clinical history upon a change in health plans 
places patients at risk of irreversible harm. Compelling a stabilized patient to abandon an 
effective regimen, or forcing them to retry a medication that has already proven clinically 
ineffective or intolerable under a prior payer, directly undermines patient safety. While the 
agency’s advancement of the Payer-to-Payer Application Programming Interface (API) 
represents a vital architectural improvement to address this fragmentation, the mere passive 
availability of this infrastructure is insufficient to alleviate provider burden or protect patient 
access. To realize the transformative potential of interoperability, CMS must ensure payers 
across public and commercial markets actively ingest and apply this API-transmitted data. 
Through the reciprocal acceptance of this clinical history, payers could programmatically 
identify therapies a patient has already tried and failed, thereby auto-granting corresponding 
prior authorizations and eliminating the hazardous, wasteful practice of restarting step therapy 
protocols. 
To structurally safeguard this continuity of care, payers should honor historical step therapy 
determinations. This principle reflects broad consensus across the healthcare continuum; a 2021 
multi-stakeholder roundtable convened by the National Pharmaceutical Council affirmed that 
treatment steps completed under a preceding health plan should be recognized upon transitioning 
coverage.13 Additionally, when considering under what conditions a step therapy exception 
should be granted, CMS should anchor to clear specific instances that include when: 
●​ the patient already tried and failed on the step therapy protocol or it is contraindicated; 
●​ the step therapy protocol is expected to be ineffective and delaying effective treatment 
would lead to severe or irreversible health consequences; 
●​ the step therapy protocol will prevent the patient from fulfilling daily or occupational 
duties; or 
●​ the patient is stable on their current medication. 
13 Karmarkar T, Dubois RW, Graff JS. Stakeholders find that step therapy should be evidence-based, flexible, and 
transparent: assessing appropriateness using a consensus approach. J Managed Care Spec Pharm. 
2021;27(2):268–75. https://doi.org/10.18553/jmcp.2021.27.2.268. 
5 
 
Furthermore, to fully operationalize these protections for stabilized beneficiaries, the agency 
should extend the regulatory "look-back" period used in Part D to define a "new start" patient 
from 108 days to 365 days and extend this to all segments including commercial plans, ensuring 
that a patient's documented clinical journey seamlessly and securely travels with them. 
CMS Should Establish Strict Clinical Guardrails, Prohibit Off-Label Step Therapy, and 
Oversee AI-Driven Coverage Determinations 
To ensure that utilization management serves as a safeguard for appropriate care rather than an 
arbitrary barrier, CMS must enforce oversight over the clinical parameters governing these tools. 
For example, CMS should prohibit the implementation of off-label step therapy, precluding 
health plans from requiring patients to try unapproved alternatives when an FDA-approved, 
on-label medication is prescribed. Coverage criteria must also be anchored in consensus-based, 
peer-reviewed clinical guidelines, rather than the isolated financial directives of internal 
pharmacy committees. Furthermore, we urge CMS to continue to monitor the rapid integration of 
artificial intelligence (AI) and automated algorithms into the adjudication of coverage claims. 
Recent survey data from the American Medical Association indicates escalating physician alarm 
over algorithmic systems generating unwarranted, high-volume prior authorization denials with 
negligible clinical oversight.14 CMS must assert regulatory scrutiny over AI-driven claims 
management to ensure patient access is not deferred to opaque technological models. We 
recommend that CMS ensure algorithms and AI are only utilized to approve care or predict 
baseline clinical pathways, and that any denial of coverage must involve a meaningful, 
documented human clinical review by a peer specialist. 
 
*​
*​
*​
*​
* 
 
Thank you for the opportunity to provide input on the Proposed Rule. We would welcome the 
opportunity to answer any questions CMS may have regarding our comments. 
Sincerely,

# Comment Analysis Template: CMS-2026-1255-0001

## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Genentech, Inc.; signed by Dan Neves, Senior Director, U.S. Policy and Evidence.
- **Stakeholder type:** Other / Manufacturer
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** Genentech describes itself as the original biotech company with 50 years of history, more than 40 approved U.S. medicines, 66 new molecules in clinical development, and 43 FDA Breakthrough Therapy Designations. It incorporates by reference PhRMA's broader comments and focuses this letter on the step therapy RFI.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Genentech focuses on step therapy and argues that opaque, inflexible utilization management increasingly delays access to clinically appropriate drugs, worsens disparities, and imposes administrative costs. It recommends public step therapy metrics, a ban on embedded step therapy disguised as PA, therapeutic-area disaggregation, active use of Payer-to-Payer API history, recognition of prior step therapy determinations, clear exceptions, a 365-day look-back period, prohibition of off-label step therapy, evidence-based criteria, and human peer review for AI-driven denials.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** API-USAGE-METRICS; Payer-to-Payer API aspects of FHIR-IG-REQUIRED; GENERAL/RFI on step therapy; PA-DENIAL-REASONS/PA reform indirectly; PATIENT-ACCESS and TRANSPARENCY themes.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** 91 Fed. Reg. 19890; RIN 0938-AV44; CMS-0062-P.
- **Standards referenced:** Payer-to-Payer API; artificial intelligence/algorithms in claims management. No specific FHIR IGs, NCPDP standards, or CFR sections are named in the substantive recommendations.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Public step therapy metrics and embedded step therapy**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL/RFI / API-USAGE-METRICS
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Plans may hide treatment-sequence mandates inside standard PA criteria, making formularies opaque and blocking access to therapies.
- **Specific request:** Require public reporting of step therapy metrics with the rigor proposed for PA metrics and categorically prohibit embedded step therapy protocols within ordinary PA criteria.

**Topic 2: Therapeutic-area disaggregation of utilization management data**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS / TRANSPARENCY
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Aggregate reporting can obscure localized inequities and disease-specific access problems.
- **Specific request:** Require plans to disaggregate utilization management data by specific therapeutic areas.

**Topic 3: Payer-to-Payer API use for continuity of care**
- **Provision ID:** FHIR-IG-REQUIRED / API-USAGE-METRICS / GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Passive availability of API-transmitted history is insufficient if payers do not ingest and apply it to identify therapies already tried and failed.
- **Specific request:** Require payers across public and commercial markets to actively ingest and apply Payer-to-Payer API data to programmatically identify prior treatment failures and auto-grant corresponding authorizations.

**Topic 4: Honor historical step therapy determinations**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL/RFI
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Forcing a stable patient to repeat a failed or intolerable drug after changing plans undermines patient safety and can cause irreversible harm.
- **Specific request:** Require payers to honor step therapy determinations completed under a prior health plan.

**Topic 5: Step therapy exception standards**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL/RFI
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Exceptions are needed when a protocol is clinically inappropriate, harmful, or disruptive to stability and functioning.
- **Specific request:** Require exceptions when the patient already tried and failed the protocol or it is contraindicated; when the protocol is expected to be ineffective and delay would cause severe or irreversible consequences; when it prevents daily or occupational functioning; or when the patient is stable on current medication.

**Topic 6: Look-back period for “new start” status**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL/RFI
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** A short look-back period can cause stabilized patients to be treated as new starts and forced into repeat step therapy.
- **Specific request:** Extend the Part D look-back period from 108 days to 365 days and apply it across all segments, including commercial plans.

**Topic 7: Prohibition on off-label step therapy**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL/RFI
- **Position:** Oppose off-label step therapy
- **Rationale:** Plans should not require patients to try unapproved alternatives when an FDA-approved on-label medicine is prescribed.
- **Specific request:** Prohibit off-label step therapy.

**Topic 8: Evidence-based coverage criteria**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL/RFI
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Coverage criteria should be clinically grounded rather than driven by internal pharmacy committee financial directives.
- **Specific request:** Anchor criteria in consensus-based, peer-reviewed clinical guidelines.

**Topic 9: AI-driven claims management**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL/RFI
- **Position:** Modify
- **Rationale:** Algorithmic systems may generate high-volume denials without adequate clinical oversight.
- **Specific request:** Require regulatory scrutiny of AI claims management; permit AI/algorithms only to approve care or predict clinical pathways, and require meaningful documented human clinical review by a peer specialist for any denial.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S29/S35:** Recommends public reporting of step therapy metrics and disaggregation by therapeutic area, analogous to PA transparency requirements.
- **S66-S82:** Responds to the step therapy RFI extensively, including transparency, continuity of care, exceptions, look-back periods, clinical guidelines, off-label step therapy, and AI-driven denials.
- **S53/S54/S55 (indirect):** Although framed as step therapy, the request for active Payer-to-Payer API use and human review of AI-driven denials implicates implementation and enforcement mechanisms for interoperable payer data exchange.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Require public reporting of step therapy metrics.
2. Prohibit embedding step therapy protocols within standard prior authorization criteria.
3. Require utilization management data to be disaggregated by therapeutic area.
4. Require payers to actively ingest and apply Payer-to-Payer API data to identify prior failed therapies.
5. Honor historical step therapy determinations from preceding health plans.
6. Grant step therapy exceptions when prior failure, contraindication, expected ineffectiveness, severe or irreversible harm, impaired daily/occupational function, or patient stability is present.
7. Extend the Part D “new start” look-back period from 108 days to 365 days and apply it to all segments, including commercial plans.
8. Prohibit off-label step therapy.
9. Anchor coverage criteria in consensus-based, peer-reviewed clinical guidelines.
10. Scrutinize AI-driven claims management and require meaningful documented human peer-specialist review before any denial.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Opaque step therapy, embedded restrictions disguised as PA, failure to honor clinical history across payers, off-label step therapy, non-evidence-based criteria, and AI-generated denials without clinical review.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Treatment delays, clinical deterioration, rapid disease progression, health inequities, patient financial exposure, benefit abandonment, clinician burden, burnout, and administrative costs.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Passive rather than active use of Payer-to-Payer API data, lack of public step therapy reporting, formulary opacity, coverage criteria extending beyond FDA labels, and algorithmic denial systems.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** Up to 56% of Part D brand drugs are subject to utilization controls; commercial insurers deny initial coverage for three out of four patients across key chronic disease states; treatment gaps average three to five weeks; some patients must cycle through up to ten alternative therapies; 94% of MA providers report step therapy restricts access to preferred physician-administered Part B treatments; 56% of Black Americans and 60% of Hispanic Americans experience UM restrictions versus 36% of white Americans; 93% of physicians report care delays and 89% report burnout; estimated $93 billion annual ecosystem cost to navigate and contest UM; Part D sponsors required PA for certain breast cancer treatments 97% of the time and embedded step therapy in up to 88% of those cases.
- **Studies or research referenced:** Avalere analyses on Part D and MA step therapy; IQVIA reports; Rucker et al. Health Affairs 2025; PhRMA patient experience data; AMA prior authorization surveys; Howell et al. Health Affairs 2021; American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network analysis; National Pharmaceutical Council roundtable / Karmarkar et al. JMCP 2021.
- **Examples provided:** Breast cancer treatments, commercial chronic disease therapies, preferred physician-administered Part B treatments, severe/progressive/autoimmune conditions, FDA-approved on-label treatments, and AI/algorithmic PA denials.

## 9. IMPACT ASSESSMENT

- **Affected stakeholders:** Patients using complex medicines, oncology and chronic disease patients, Medicare Part D and MA beneficiaries, commercial plan members, prescribers, payers, manufacturers, and marginalized populations.
- **Economic implications:** Genentech argues current UM imposes large administrative costs and can shift costs to patients when coverage barriers force out-of-pocket payment.
- **Technical feasibility:** Depends on payers actively ingesting and using Payer-to-Payer API data rather than merely making it available; also depends on enforceable reporting and AI oversight.
- **Patient care impact:** High; the letter frames step therapy as causing delayed appropriate treatment, disease progression, and inequitable access.

## 10. SENTIMENT ANALYSIS

- **Overall position:** Concerned / Supportive of reform
- **Tone:** Critical, evidence-driven, policy-focused
- **Priority level:** High

## 11. KEY QUOTES

1. "Genentech supports and incorporates by reference herein the policy and other arguments detailed in the comments on this proposed rule filed by the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America." - Context: Scope of comments and alignment with PhRMA.
2. "CMS should require plans to publicly report step therapy metrics with the same rigor proposed for prior authorization, and categorically prohibit the embedding of step therapy protocols within otherwise typical prior authorization criteria." - Context: Transparency recommendation.
3. "The mere passive availability of this infrastructure is insufficient to alleviate provider burden or protect patient access." - Context: Payer-to-Payer API continuity recommendation.
4. "Any denial of coverage must involve a meaningful, documented human clinical review by a peer specialist." - Context: AI-driven claims management recommendation.

## 12. THEMES

- [x] **PROVIDER-BURDEN** - The comment cites administrative friction, physician burnout, and burdens from opaque UM.
- [x] **HEALTH-EQUITY** - The letter cites disproportionate UM restrictions affecting Black and Hispanic Americans.
- [x] **TECHNICAL-FEASIBILITY** - The Payer-to-Payer API recommendation depends on active payer ingestion and programmatic use of prior therapy history.
- [x] **PATIENT-ACCESS** - Central focus is reducing access delays and preventing patients from repeating failed therapies.
- [x] **TRANSPARENCY** - Strongly supports public step therapy metrics, disaggregated reporting, and prohibition of hidden embedded step therapy.
- [x] **EXISTING-WORKFLOWS** - Discusses current UM/PA workflows and how step therapy can be hidden within PA criteria.
- [x] **STAKEHOLDER-COORDINATION** - Requires continuity across prior and current payers and use of Payer-to-Payer API history.
- [x] **REGULATORY-AUTHORITY** - Asks CMS to create enforceable rules for step therapy, AI denials, and clinical criteria.
